titulo.en: I would like a coffee, please

objetivo.en: Politely order a drink or something to eat in a café and ask for the check.

nota.en: The polite way to order. Softer than saying “I want”.
Mí has an accent mark; it is not the same as mi (my).
The j is a strong h: “HOO-go”.
Un jugo de naranja = an orange juice.
The accent mark keeps it apart from te (you).

explicacion.en: After para, use mí, not yo: para mí means “for me”. Mí always has an accent mark.
Cuenta is feminine, so it takes la: la cuenta.
With a waitress you don't know, use the formal form: trae, not traes. Traes is the form for a friend.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: j and soft g

texto.en: The letter j, and the letter g before e or i (ge, gi), sounds like a strong English h, a little rougher than the h in “hello”: jugo is “HOO-go”, naranja is “nah-RAHN-hah”, Jorge is “HOR-heh”, gente is “HEN-teh”. Before a, o or u, the g is the hard g of “go”. Say them slowly: jugo, naranja, Jorge, gente.

In Spanish, the polite way to order is quisiera + what you want: Quisiera un café, por favor (“I would like a coffee, please”). It sounds softer than “I want”. You can also ask with a question: ¿Me da…? (“Could I have…?”) or ¿Me trae…? (“Could you bring me…?”). The waitress, la mesera, is someone you don't know, so you use the formal form of the verb: da and trae. If two people are ordering, the waitress asks ¿Qué desean? (“What would you like?”). Use para mí to order for yourself: Para mí, un jugo de naranja (“For me, an orange juice”). When you finish, ask for the check: ¿Me trae la cuenta, por favor? She answers Enseguida (“Right away”). Emma and Andrés use tú with each other, but both use the formal form with the waitress.

objetivo.en: Ask the price of one or several things and understand prices in dollars and cents.

traduccion.en: how much does it cost? (one thing)

nota.en: For one thing: ¿Cuánto cuesta el pan?

traduccion.en: how much do they cost? (several things)

nota.en: For several things: ¿Cuánto cuestan las galletas?
Asks for the total of everything you buy.
Plural: los dólares. Ecuador uses the U.S. dollar.
Plural: los centavos. One dollar = cien centavos.
The c before i sounds like s.

explicacion.en: Galletas is plural, so the verb is plural too: cuestan. One thing: cuesta; several things: cuestan.
You may also hear ¿Cuánto es el pan? in everyday speech, but in this course ask the price of one item with ¿Cuánto cuesta…? ¿Cuánto es? asks for the total of everything you buy.
After a number bigger than one, the noun is plural: cincuenta centavos, dos dólares.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: c, z and s

texto.en: In Latin America, s, z and c before e or i all sound like the English s in “sun”: centavos, cincuenta, precio, dólares, zapato. There is no English “th” sound in these letters (that is only in parts of Spain). Careful: c before a, o or u is a hard k: cuesta, cuánto, café. Say them slowly: precio, centavos, cincuenta, cuesta.

titulo.en: Asking the price: cuesta and cuestan

texto.en: English says “How much is the bread?”, but Spanish uses the verb costar (to cost): ¿Cuánto cuesta el pan? (“How much does the bread cost?”). The verb agrees with the thing you ask about: one thing, cuesta (¿Cuánto cuesta el pan?); several things, cuestan (¿Cuánto cuestan las galletas?). The answer uses the same verb: Cuesta cincuenta centavos. Cuestan setenta y cinco centavos. To ask for the total of everything you buy, use ¿Cuánto es?; the answer begins with Son: Son un dólar con veinticinco (“It's $1.25”). Ecuador uses the U.S. dollar: un dólar, dos dólares (the plural adds -es), un centavo, cincuenta centavos (the plural adds -s). You already know the numbers from 21 to 100, such as setenta y cinco. Emma uses usted with doña Carmen, who uses tú with Emma.
Dollars and cents are joined with con. Tap each phrase to hear it.

objetivo.en: Pay in cash or by card, ask how you can pay and understand the change.

nota.en: A regular -ar verb: pago, pagas, paga.
Say en, not con: pago en efectivo.
The v sounds like a soft b: “BWEL-to”.

explicacion.en: In English you pay “by card”, but in Spanish you pay con tarjeta (with a card).
For cash, Spanish says en efectivo (in cash), not con.
Pagar is the infinitive. With yo, use pago.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: b and v

texto.en: In Spanish, the letters b (be) and v (uve) sound exactly the same, like an English b. At the start of a word, as in vuelto or bien, it is a plain b; between vowels, as in efectivo, the lips barely touch. There is no English “v” sound with the teeth on the lip. Say them slowly: bien, vuelto, efectivo, vemos.

Use en efectivo for cash (“in cash”) and con tarjeta for a card (“with a card”): Pago en efectivo. Pago con tarjeta. Pagar is a regular -ar verb: see the table below. To ask whether you can pay a certain way, use ¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta? (“Can I pay by card?”); puedo means “I can”. A shop that only takes cash says Solo en efectivo (“Cash only”). El vuelto is the change, the money that comes back to you. A clerk who uses usted with you says Aquí está su vuelto; a person who uses tú says Aquí está tu vuelto, like doña Carmen with Emma. El dinero is money in general. Remember that la tarjeta is feminine.

objetivo.en: Ask for and describe clothes by color, making the color agree with the noun.

nota.en: Feminine: amarilla. The ll sounds like the y in “yes”.
Same for masculine and feminine. Plural: verdes.
Same for masculine and feminine. Plural: azules.

traduccion.en: the pants / the pair of pants

explicacion.en: The color agrees with the noun. Camiseta is feminine, so the color is feminine too: roja.
In Spanish the color goes after the noun: una camiseta roja (literally “a T-shirt red”).
The color is plural when the noun is plural: camisetas verdes.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: ll and y

texto.en: In most of Latin America, ll and y sound the same, like the y in “yes”: amarillo is “ah-mah-REE-yo”, amarilla is “ah-mah-REE-yah”, and yo is “yo”. When y stands alone it means “and” and sounds like the ee in “see”: té y pastel. Say them slowly: yo, amarillo, amarilla.

titulo.en: Colors go after the noun and agree with it

texto.en: Colors are adjectives. In Spanish the color goes after the noun, and it agrees with it in gender and number: una camiseta roja (literally “a T-shirt red”), un pantalón negro. Colors ending in -o have four forms: rojo, roja, rojos, rojas (the same for blanco, negro and amarillo). Colors ending in -e or in a consonant, like verde and azul, have one form for masculine and feminine: un pantalón verde, una camiseta verde. In the plural they add -s or -es: verdes, azules. Check the gender of the clothes: la camiseta and la chaqueta are feminine, and el pantalón is masculine. In Latin America, un pantalón (singular) is common for “a pair of pants”. Emma and the shop assistant use usted with each other.
Colors in -o have four forms. Verde and azul have only singular and plural. Tap each form to hear it.
Un goes with masculine nouns and una with feminine nouns. Tap each phrase to hear it.

titulo.en: This, that, that over there: do you have another size?

objetivo.en: Point out items near or far away with este, ese and aquel, ask their price and ask for another size.

nota.en: Feminine: aquella. The u is silent: “ah-KEL”.
Near you, or not far away.
Feminine: pequeña. Talla pequeña = small size.

explicacion.en: The demonstrative agrees with the noun. Camiseta is feminine: esta, esa, aquella.
Camiseta is feminine, so use esta, not este.
With a shop assistant you don't know, use the formal form: ¿Tiene…? Use ¿Tienes…? with a friend.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: qu and gu

texto.en: In que, qui, gue and gui, the letter u is silent. The qu sounds like k, and the gu (before e or i) is a hard g: aquel is “ah-KEL”, aquí is “ah-KEE”, ¿qué? is “keh”, and guitarra is “gee-TAH-rrah”. Say them slowly: qué, aquel, aquella, aquí, guitarra.

titulo.en: Pointing: this, that, that over there

texto.en: Spanish has three words for pointing, depending on where the thing is. Este, esta mean “this”, near me (aquí). Ese, esa mean “that”, near you or not far away (ahí). Aquel, aquella mean “that over there”, far from both of you (allí). English has only “this” and “that”, so aquel is the extra one. They agree with the noun: este, ese, aquel with masculine nouns (este pantalón), and esta, esa, aquella with feminine nouns (esta camiseta, aquella chaqueta). To ask for another size, say ¿Tiene otra talla? with a shop assistant (formal) and ¿Tienes otra talla? with a friend. A size is la talla: talla pequeña (small) and talla grande (large). Emma and the shop assistant use usted with each other.
Three words for three distances. Tap each phrase to hear it.
